title: Doom of the House of Duryea

knight_criteria.rationale: The story pseudo-scientifically frames hereditary vampirism as a heritable condition explained in quasi-scholarly terms, with references to shaking science 'to its very foundation.' However this is presented as demonic/supernatural (vrykolakas) rather than genuine speculative science, so materiality of an actual scientific representation is uncertain.
No engineered device, technique, or invention materially affects the setting or outcome. Ropes and a shotgun are ordinary tools, not inventions driving the plot in any technological sense.
The story is set in a contemporary 'civilized century' with historical references to ancestors, but there is no speculative future, remote past setting, or temporal displacement.

The tale develops systematic consequences from a stated premise (a hereditary vampire needing a family 'medium' whose proximity triggers metamorphosis), and the plot unfolds these rules to their fatal conclusion. Whether this counts as extrapolation from an identifiable scientific/social premise versus supernatural legend is uncertain.

Coroners and savants examine the bloodless corpses but explicitly cannot explain or test the phenomenon; no hypothesis-testing, measurement, or evidential revision materially drives understanding or action. The characters read a book rather than apply the scientific method.
There are no other planets, dimensions, nonordinary cosmic environments, or visitors from them; the demonic 'presence' is a supernatural/psychic conceit set entirely on Earth.

The deaths are personal tragedies—a father drained of blood and a son's suicide—confined to the last of a family line. Despite being fatal, they lack the large-scale (natural, technological, cosmic, biological, human-caused) disaster scope required; this is personal misfortune, not catastrophe.
